title: There's no such thing as AI art
subtitle: AI can create beauty, but not meaning
author: Derek Matravers
introduction: AI can now imitate the great artists so well that we often can’t tell the difference. But imitation is not creation. Philosopher of aesthetics Derek Matravers argues that a painting without intention is not art at all. When we engage with a painting merely for its beauty, the maker’s identity might not matter. But art does more: it connects us to another mind, to an artist’s deliberate creation of meaning. A human artist stakes something on each decision; an AI stakes nothing, merely averaging out its training data. It might make some beautiful objects, but they are empty of the meaning that we seek in art.
body:
Can AI produce art? The question is not as simple as it might seem. Certainly, AI has played a large part in the production of works of art. The Turkish-American artist, Refik Anadol, has won international acclaim for some spectacular pieces of visual art generated by AI. But was it Anadol who produced these using AI akin to Titian producing his paintings using a paintbrush? Or was it AI who produced these? If consciousness is necessary for creativity, and AI lacks consciousness, then AI lacks creativity. And if creativity is necessary to produce art, then AI could not have produced the works and those works still be art. These and other questions are generating a rich and interesting debate in universities and academic journals across the world.

Where one stands on these matters will depend on where one stands on the broader issues that structure the debate. There is no point in asking whether AI can produce art if one does not know what art is. The same might be true for other concepts that feature in the debate, such as intentions, creativity, meaning and so on. It also helps to know about how the various systems (in particular, the image-generating systems such as DALL-E, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion) work. I am going to start at a rather more practical level. AI can produce works that have the appearance of works of art in all media. It can produce complex narrative works, complex musical works, and complex images. Judged purely on qualities associated with the medium (say, narrative, musical, or visual complexity) some of these works are above the quality most of us could achieve if we tried it ourselves.

We need not discriminate between AI-produced work and human-produced work; it depends on what achievements we are trying to understand.

Say someone tried an experiment (indeed, I would be surprised if this has not already been done). We tell AI to produce a novel in the style of Agatha Christie, a concerto in the style of Vivaldi, and a painting in the style of Titian. We would need to fiddle around a bit for the painting, as it would need to be oil on canvas, but let’s assume that could all be done. We then find some group of vaguely expert people, give them the AI-produced object together with some actual Agatha Christies, concerti by Vivaldi, and works by Titian, and ask for them to be ranked against each other in terms of quality. I say “vaguely expert” so that, were the fake easy to spot, they would spot it, but they would not be able to spot the fake simply because they know the various oeuvres so well they would know immediately which was the odd one out. I shall assume, which is the answer I would expect, that the AI-produced work did no better or worse than the real things.

Now this seems to present us with a problem which is independent of the question of whether what AI has produced is art. When engaging with art, or art-like objects, do we have reason to engage with the real things over engaging with the AI-produced things? Once again, this question is not as simple as it might seem.

The reason this is not simple is that we engage with works of art (I shall assume, for the sake of ease of exposition, that what the AI produced are works of art) for different purposes. For some of these purposes, being produced by AI does not matter; for others it might; and for yet others it does. I will start with some purposes where it does not matter. Sometimes our purpose is to engage with the aesthetically relevant appearance properties the work has to offer. On many such occasions, AI-produced works will do as well as, possibly even better than, human-produced works.

There is nothing wrong with engaging with art for these purposes. Indeed, sometimes such engagement is obviously sensible: reading a book to pass the time in an entertaining fashion, having the music on as background to a dinner party, or using the image to front a Christmas card being examples. However, the engagement can also be complex and multi-faceted. For example, one might find an image compelling; it might depict a dramatic state of affairs, the drama amplified by its formal properties (its dynamism, say, produced by a combination of dramatic swirls and vivid colors). One might be bowled over by the intricacy of the structure of a piece of music or by the narrative complexity of a story. If one is engaging with a work of art for the purposes of engaging with these properties, the properties available in mere appearance, it does not matter whether they were produced by AI or by some human being.

There is a tempting line of thought, endorsed by a long philosophical tradition, that this is the right way to engage with a work of art. This is motivated by the following kind of thought experiment. Suppose you came across some book, piece of music, or image and were captivated by it. You spent time engaging with it, encouraged others to engage with it, singing its praises to anyone who would listen. Then you discover that it was not, as you thought, produced by some human being but by AI. What should you do? Nothing in the appearance of the work has changed. What reason would you have to downgrade your opinion? If you do think this is the right way to engage with a work, you have no reason to prioritize art produced by human beings over art produced by AI.

Obviously, you would have reason to downgrade your opinion if the purpose of your engaging with the work did require it to be produced by a human being. For example, your purpose in engaging with a work might include attempting to understand what the artist was trying to achieve with the work. For example, engaging with Gauguin’s works from his period in Tahiti might include attempting to understand his response to modernity, colonialism, sexuality, and his trying to find his way out of the dead-end of impressionism. If this is your purpose in engaging with art, then you would be right to downgrade your opinion of a work on discovering it was created by AI. In creating works, AI is not (yet) attempting the kinds of achievement that are the content of this kind of understanding. Although AI is not (yet) attempting this kind of achievement, there are some kinds of achievement distinctive to AI—or at least the use of AI. For example, Anadol’s series of worksMachine Hallucinations is the result of the machine being “trained on” specific visual data sets—for example, 300 million photos of New York. The final works therefore are remediations of (responses to) this data in ways that would be impossible for any human being. Attempting to understand the work is, in part, attempting to understand this AI remediation. This does not show that we need not discriminate between AI-produced work and human-produced work; it depends on what achievements we are trying to understand. Furthermore, it might be that to think of achievements at all requires a contribution of a human artist—that is, Machine Hallucinations is Anadol’s achievement via AI.

The most dramatic argument that we should reserve our engagement with art to that produced by humans comes from Richard Wollheim. So far, I have talked as if what can be said about one art medium can be said about any other; I have moved, without comment, between narrative, music, and the visual arts. However, sometimes this cannot be done; most prominently when talking about meaning. What is the meaning of a sentence—say, “the bull is in the field”? As language speakers, we can work this out from knowledge of the individual words and the way they are put together to make sentences. There are all kinds of complexities to keep philosophers of language busy, but, in a sense, there is no problem with linguistic meaning. Contrast this with the question “what is the meaning of Mozart’s Piano Concerto in A Major?” This is not a stupid question, and there is no shortage of theories about how to answer it. But the answer is not obvious; indeed, it is not obvious that there is an answer in any straightforward sense of “meaning.” Now consider the meaning of a painting. What does Manet’s Madame Brunet mean?

You might just think the question makes no sense. If it does make sense, the answer is along the lines of: it is a painting of a young woman, with hat and gloves, in a dark dress. If something along those lines was the answer, then AI could produce paintings with meanings as AI could, without problem, produce a painting of a young woman, with hat and gloves, in a dark dress. Not for Richard Wollheim, who thought paintings had complex meanings that were related to, and far outstripped, their depictive content. Where does Wollheim get his account of how paintings can have meanings? There is no analogous story to language having a meaning. Wollheim’s answer was that what it is for a painting to have meaning is for the marks of the painting to have been made with a deliberate act of intention. Discovering the meaning is a matter of retrieving the creative process that resulted in the painting being as it in fact is. What, then, would Wollheim make of a painting produced by AI? In terms of its meaning as a work of art, there would, literally, be nothing that could be made of it. For Wollheim, there is no raw material for interpretation. He would not deny that what he saw in front of him was an image of a horse, or a ship, or whatever. It is only that the object was not a painting—at least as that term is understood to pick out something that is art.

SUGGESTED VIEWING AI and the creativity crisis With Niki Seth-Smith, Martha Fiennes, John Ralston Saul, Judith Donath

If one takes Wollheim’s view, as I do, then to claim that AI produces paintings that are art is to commit a category mistake—akin to saying that chalk is hungry or thoughts are purple. Paintings simply are those objects that are the vehicles of human intention and the quality of the painting is some function of the quality of that intention. It may still be that AI can produce objects that are worth our investing time and effort in appreciating and understanding. It might even produce objects that are worth our investing time and effort in appreciating and understanding that look like paintings. However, it cannot produce paintings because paintings, in our culture, simply are those things that are vehicles for intention.
